l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: Dr. John Watson accompanied Josiah Amberley to Little Purlington and ensured that he actually made the journey. His observations of the smell of paint and the theatre seat number helped Holmes establish that Amberley's story and alibi were false.

l: Josiah Amberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: Josiah Amberley was a miser, a jealous chess player, and the husband of the missing woman. Holmes concluded that Amberley had murdered his wife and Dr. Ray Ernest by trapping them in the strong-room and flooding it with gas; Amberley was arrested after trying to swallow a white pellet.

l: Amberley's wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: Amberley's wife was made wretched by his niggardly ways and became involved with Dr. Ray Ernest. Holmes concluded that Amberley murdered her in the strong-room.

l: Dr. Ray Ernest, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: Dr. Ray Ernest was a chess-playing doctor whom Holmes identified as Amberley's wife's companion. Holmes concluded that Amberley murdered him along with Amberley's wife.

l: Mr. Barker, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: Mr. Barker was a private investigator engaged by Dr. Ray Ernest's family. He independently suspected foul play, confronted Holmes while Holmes was entering Amberley's house, then helped Holmes restrain Amberley and took charge of formalities at the station.

l: Inspector MacKinnon, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: Inspector MacKinnon represented the police and objected that Holmes's irregular methods had taken credit from the official investigation. He accepted Holmes's evidence, arranged a search, and was credited by the newspaper with deductions and discoveries that Holmes had actually made.

l: Amberley's wife and Dr. Ray Ernest, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: Amberley's wife and Dr. Ray Ernest were the couple whose disappearance Holmes investigated. Holmes concluded that they had been murdered by Amberley in the strong-room, and their bodies were expected to be found in a disused well.

l: the police, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The police had formed their own views of the case and were prepared to arrest Amberley. Three constables were sent to search the house, and the police took over the investigation after Holmes supplied his findings.

l: Little Purlington, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: Little Purlington was a remote village in Essex on a branch line, reached by a slow train and a two-mile drive. Holmes used it as the destination for the forged telegram so Amberley could not return promptly to his house.

l: the Vicarage, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The Vicarage at Little Purlington was the address named in the forged telegram. Its vicar, J. C. Elman, denied sending the telegram and said he had never heard of Amberley.

l: The Adventure of the Retired Colourman, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The case concerned the disappearance of Amberley's wife and Dr. Ray Ernest, along with securities that Amberley said had been taken. It culminated in Amberley's arrest and the discovery of evidence that the disappearances were murders rather than an elopement.

l: the murders, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The murders were planned by Amberley out of jealousy and revenge. Holmes believed he lured the victims into the strong-room, sealed them inside, and killed them by releasing gas.

l: the forged telegram, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The forged telegram summoned Amberley to the Vicarage with a promise of information about his recent loss. Holmes arranged it to remove Amberley from the house while Holmes searched it.

l: the strong-room, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The strong-room had an iron door and shutter and could be sealed almost hermetically. Holmes found that it contained the end of an open gas pipe, making it the likely death-chamber.

l: the gas pipe, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The gas pipe ran along the skirting, rose into the wall, and entered the strong-room. It ended openly in a ceiling rose, allowing the room to be flooded with gas from an outside tap.

l: the gas, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: Gas was released into the sealed strong-room, where Holmes said a person would have less than two minutes of conscious sensation. Its smell was partly concealed by the smell of paint.

l: green paint, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The strong smell of paint was one of the first clues. Holmes inferred that Amberley was using it to conceal another smell, which he identified as the smell of gas connected with the murders.

l: the two bodies, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The two bodies were those of Amberley's wife and Dr. Ray Ernest. Holmes directed the police to search the cellars and garden, especially for a disused well where the bodies could not be far away.

l: the disused well, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The disused well was identified by Holmes as the likely place where the two bodies had been hidden. The newspaper later reported that the bodies were found there, concealed by a dog-kennel.

l: the wall message, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The wall message was written in purple indelible pencil just above the skirting in the strong-room. It read only 'We we----', which Holmes interpreted as the beginning of 'We were murdered.'

l: the suicide attempt, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes, In the morning I was up betimes, but some toast crumbs and two empty
s: The suicide attempt occurred when Amberley tried to swallow a white pellet after Holmes asked what he had done with the bodies. Holmes restrained him and forced the matter to proceed through the proper legal process.

l: The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: This document is a prefaced collection of Sherlock Holmes cases, framed by Arthur Conan Doyle’s farewell to Holmes and Watson. Doyle recalls Holmes’s progress from A Study in Scarlet and The Sign of Four through the Strand stories, explains that public demand brought Holmes back after The Memoirs, and thanks readers. The cases follow Holmes, usually with Dr. John Watson, through crimes, disappearances, threats, and apparent supernatural mysteries. Holmes prevents Violet de Merville’s marriage to the corrupt Baron Adelbert Gruner by obtaining Gruner’s incriminating record of women he ruined; Kitty Winter disfigures Gruner and the marriage is canceled. He finds that the secretly confined Godfrey Emsworth has non-infective pseudo-leprosy rather than leprosy, recovers the Mazarin Stone from Count Negretto Sylvius and Sam Merton, and protects Mrs. Maberley after Isadora Klein orders the destruction of Douglas Maberley’s manuscript. Several cases overturn misleading appearances: the supposed Sussex vampire is a mother removing poison after Jacky Ferguson attacks a baby; John Garrideb is the criminal James Winter, alias Killer Evans, seeking a counterfeiting cellar; and Miss Grace Dunbar is cleared when Holmes proves that Mrs. Gibson engineered evidence around her own death. Holmes discovers that Professor Presbury’s animal-like behavior comes from a rejuvenation treatment involving black-faced Langur serum, and that Fitzroy McPherson was killed accidentally by Cyanea capillata, the “Lion’s Mane,” rather than by Ian Murdoch. Later, Eugenia Ronder confesses her part in a plot against her abusive husband, ending the Abbas Parva matter; Holmes uncovers Lady Beatrice Falder’s death and Mr. Norlett’s impersonation of her at Shoscombe Old Place; and, in the final case, he exposes Josiah Amberley’s fabricated story that his wife and Dr. Ray Ernest fled with his money. Amberley had murdered them in his strong-room, but Holmes, police, and Inspector MacKinnon arrest him and stop his attempted suicide. Across the collection, Holmes repeatedly uses observation, disguises, experiments, and psychological pressure to reveal concealed motives and protect the innocent.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Sherlock Holmes is an imaginary, famous consulting and private detective, a professional investigator whose adventures debut in A Study in Scarlet and The Sign of Four. Based at Baker Street for much of his active practice, he works closely with Dr. John Watson, his friend, companion, confidential partner, and frequent assistant. Holmes is defined by logical analysis, intellectual deduction, acute senses, an unusually retentive memory for trifles, trained observation, and a habit of using his head rather than his heart. He maintains confidential records, seeks no public credit, represents justice through his work, and uses associates such as Shinwell Johnson, Langdale Pike, Mercer, and the police when useful. His characteristic possessions and methods include pipes, a tobacco-slipper, a notebook and index volume, disguises, practical jokes, forensic microscopy, staged deceptions, and direct personal risk. The records show him facing threats, exhaustion, and injury while continuing to investigate. In the Baron Gruner matter, he tries to save Violet de Merville, is attacked and wounded, and obtains Gruner's incriminating book through a calculated burglary. He then resolves varied cases: exposing Godfrey Emsworth's condition, recovering the Mazarin Stone from Count Sylvius, protecting Mrs. Maberley from a manuscript theft, explaining the Ferguson household's supposed vampirism, uncovering James Winter's fraud against Nathan Garrideb, and proving that Mrs. Gibson framed Miss Dunbar before taking her own life. Later cases emphasize his willingness to challenge hidden wrongdoing and seemingly strange events. He traces Professor Presbury's transformation to Langur serum, identifies Cyanea capillata as the cause of deaths at the Sussex coast, responds sympathetically to the veiled lodger's confession, exposes concealment at Shoscombe Old Place, and discovers that Josiah Amberley used a sealed strong-room and gas to kill. After twenty-three years of active practice, including seventeen years of cooperation with Watson, Holmes retires to his little Sussex home, keeps bees, yet continues to investigate when summoned. A preface presents him as a popular fictional detective who was ended, revived, and finally bid farewell amid continuing public interest.

l: Dr. Watson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Dr. Watson is a physician, medical doctor, and surgeon by training; a former military doctor who served in the Indian Army; and a medical man with a not inconsiderable practice. He also played rugby for Blackheath and has a weakness for the Turkish Bath shared with Sherlock Holmes. Most importantly, he is Holmes's closest friend, old friend, longtime companion, professional and confidential partner, and habitual investigative associate. Their alliance makes Watson both an intellectual stimulus to Holmes and the narrator, biographer, and recorder of Holmes's cases, although Holmes notes that his accounts emphasize popular interest. Watson is married, and his marriage temporarily leaves Holmes without him in the unrecorded case of the blanched soldier. Across the accounts, Watson repeatedly joins Holmes at Baker Street, reads requests and referrals, travels to scenes, observes evidence, questions people, and records deductions and confessions. In the affair of the illustrious client, he helps circulate false reports of Holmes's condition, poses as Dr. Hill Barton, and distracts Baron Adelbert Gruner through supposed expertise in Chinese pottery. He later assists in urgent cases involving the Mazarin stone, The Three Gables, the Sussex vampire, the Three Garridebs, Thor Bridge, the creeping man, the veiled lodger, Shoscombe Old Place, and the retired colourman. His medical knowledge and practical action are central: he examines Ferguson's wife, identifies a human femur fragment, treats Professor Presbury's torn throat and gives morphia, recognizes prussic acid, and supplies his revolver for Holmes's Thor Bridge experiment. He is also endangered while hiding with Holmes during the Garridebs investigation, when he is shot superficially in the thigh but remains able to assist and call the Yard. His observations repeatedly furnish important clues, including paint at Amberley's house and theatre-seat details that expose Amberley's false alibi. From beginning to end, Watson is portrayed as Holmes's trusted companion and witness: active in investigations, medically capable, occasionally mistaken or uncertain, but consistently loyal, observant, and essential to preserving the cases in narrative form.

l: Arthur Conan Doyle, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Arthur Conan Doyle is the author of Sherlock Holmes. He first intended to end Holmes at the conclusion of The Memoirs, then revived him after public demand without regret. He says the lighter Holmes sketches coexisted with work in history, poetry, historical novels, psychic research, and drama.

l: Holmes's career, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Holmes's career began with A Study in Scarlet and The Sign of Four, published between 1887 and 1889, then expanded into a long short-story series beginning with A Scandal in Bohemia in 1891. Across a broken thirty-six-year run, it spans the later Victorian Era, Edward's reign, and afterward, comprising fifty-six stories in four collections plus twelve in The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes.

l: Sir James, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Sir James is a diplomat and intermediary who serves an undisclosed, illustrious client and consults Sherlock Holmes to stop Baron Gruner's marriage to Violet de Merville. Loyal and chivalrous, he explains Gruner's history, interests, address, and private telephone contact. After Holmes summons him and recounts events, Sir James takes the incriminating book and blue saucer from Holmes's room, apparently helping prevent the marriage; Watson infers that Sir James himself is the client.

l: Baron Adelbert Gruner, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Baron Adelbert Gruner is a wealthy Austrian man, forty-two, whose fortune came through shady speculations. He is remarkably handsome, with a swarthy, almost Oriental face, dark languorous eyes, raven-black hair and moustache, though his cruel, hard mouth is presented as a sign of murderous character. He is a horse fancier, a precise and tidy man, and a renowned collector and author on Chinese pottery; he owns an extensive Chinese collection. More importantly, he is portrayed as a highly dangerous antagonist: suspected of murdering his wife, connected with at least one or two further murders, and said to mistreat women by tempting, using, ruining, and discarding them. Kitty Winter says he collects ruined women as others collect moths or butterflies. Though he has a stormy past marked by bitter hatreds and accusations, he presents explanations that persuade Violet de Merville, who loves him and believes he has repented. Gruner resides at Vernon Lodge near Kingston, as well as being associated with 104 Berkeley Square, and protects his house with a burglar alarm and other precautions against Sherlock Holmes. He owns a locked brown leather book bearing his arms, written in his own hand, which records compromising romantic or sexual conduct. As he pursues and becomes engaged to Violet, intending an imminent marriage, he warns Holmes to withdraw and appears able to influence Violet against Holmes and his allies. The conflict turns when Gruner recognizes a visit by Dr. John Watson as a trap. Kitty Winter throws vitriol at him, severely burning his face, destroying one eye and badly damaging the other. While he is distracted, Holmes obtains the incriminating book despite Gruner's anti-burglary precautions. The planned marriage to Violet is canceled, and a journey to America had forced Holmes to act immediately.

l: Violet de Merville, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Violet de Merville is the young, wealthy, beautiful, accomplished, strong-willed daughter of General de Merville and fiancée of Baron Adelbert Gruner. Completely and obsessively in love with Gruner, she plans to marry him despite knowing of his stormy past and despite warnings. During Holmes and Miss Winter's visit, she is cold, self-contained, and inflexible, insisting that Gruner has repented and dismissing testimony against him. Although Holmes expects Gruner's injuries to deepen her devotion, the contents of Gruner's incriminating book bring her back to reality and lead her to reject him.

l: General de Merville, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: General de Merville, a military general of Khyber fame and Violet’s father, changes from a strong soldier into a demoralized, broken man, unable to effectively oppose Gruner over her intended marriage.

l: the illustrious client's unnamed principal, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: An unnamed, confidential client, long an intimate friend of General de Merville and a paternal figure to Violet, secretly asks Sir James Damery to engage Holmes to prevent Violet’s marriage while preserving his anonymity.

l: Shinwell Johnson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Shinwell Johnson, a former criminal who served two terms at Parkhurst, now works as Sherlock Holmes’s agent in London’s criminal underworld. Sent to find damaging information about Adelbert Gruner, he quickly locates his old mate Kitty Winter, tells her of Gruner’s pursuit of another woman, brings her to Holmes, and is tasked with taking her to a quiet suburb for protection.

l: the police, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The police are a group distinct from Scotland Yard that supports Holmes’s cases. They wait below his rooms, enter when summoned, handcuff Count Sylvius and Sam Merton, and take them away. After the burglary at The Three Gables, they examine the property, question Mrs. Maberley, take the recovered manuscript fragment, pursue the suspected gang, and investigate Sir Robert’s concealment of the death.

l: London, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_location_of Dorak [where he is supplied as an intermediary] Holmes and Watson travel from London to Camford and plan to return to London that afternoon. Dorak lives in London, where Mercer visits him at the Commercial Road.

l: Baker Street, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Baker Street contains and is the home of Sherlock Holmes. There, Holmes recovers while feigning near death, gives Dr. John Watson instructions, and receives Watson after the operation at Baron Adelbert Gruner's house. It is also where Holmes develops and later explains his theory about Ferguson's wife. Holmes meets Dr. Watson, Trevor Bennett, and later Edith Presbury there. In its final recorded episode, its bedroom exit, window, and wax dummy aid Holmes's investigation and confrontation with Count Negretto Sylvius and Sam Merton.

l: Prague, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Prague is a city and university town central to Professor Presbury’s case. He visited it before his symptoms began, and Holmes believes he learned to use a strong drug there. Dorak’s Bohemian nationality and H. Lowenstein’s correspondence about the treatment connect Prague to the serum Holmes considers central.

l: the Prague murder case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The murder of Adelbert Gruner's victim is known to Gruner's intended bride, but she treats the account as slander. Kitty also suggests that Gruner may have been connected with other murders when she recalls his remarks that certain people had died within a month.

l: the death of Baron Gruner's wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Baron Gruner's first wife died in an alleged Splügen Pass accident; Holmes believes Gruner murdered her, escaping conviction through a legal technicality and a witness's suspicious death.

l: the marriage between Baron Adelbert Gruner and Violet de Merville, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The planned marriage of Baron Adelbert Gruner and Violet de Merville becomes the central danger Holmes and his associates seek to prevent. Gruner intends to marry Violet the following month, although he is believed to have murdered his first wife and committed other wrongdoing. Violet refuses warnings, while Holmes fears she will learn Gruner’s character only after marriage and Miss Winter predicts her death. Holmes opposes the union and, after an incriminating book is used against Gruner, the marriage is prevented. Three days later, The Morning Post announces that it will not take place.

l: Chinese pottery, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Chinese pottery is studied by Dr. John Watson for roughly twenty-four hours at Sherlock Holmes’s instruction. He memorizes its ceramic periods, artists, marks, and dynasties, including Sung, Tang, Yuan, Ming, Hung-wu, and Yung-lo, to pose as an informed collector.

l: the investigation and counterplot, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: An investigation and counterplot led by Sherlock Holmes with Dr. John Watson. Sir James Damery asks Holmes to prevent Gruner's marriage to Violet. Holmes investigates and confronts Gruner, seeking underworld evidence through Shinwell Johnson. Holmes and Watson then protect Kitty Winter, deceive Gruner with a staged illness and Ming saucer, and enable her vitriol attack.

l: Kitty Winter, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Kitty Winter is a young, fiery woman and Baron Adelbert Gruner’s last former mistress. She says Gruner tempted, used, and ruined her, made her what she is, and may have murdered others; she intensely hates him and offers unpaid help to bring him down as firsthand evidence of his abuse. She joins Holmes in warning Violet de Merville, Gruner’s intended bride, that he ruins women and will cause Violet’s death, though rage nearly drives Kitty to attack Violet. After Holmes is attacked, Kitty is moved for protection, hides near Gruner’s house, and throws vitriol through his window, severely disfiguring him. She is thereafter targeted by two attackers and faces a grave vitriol-throwing prosecution.

l: Adelbert Gruner's intended bride, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Adelbert Gruner's intended bride is madly in love with him, dismisses reports of his murders as slanders, and refuses to reconsider after hearing his account and receiving his pardon.

l: Adelbert Gruner's brown leather book, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Adelbert Gruner's brown leather book is a locked, gold-armed volume kept, perhaps, in a pigeon-hole of his old bureau in the inner study. Written in Baron Adelbert Gruner's own hand, it is a compromising diary of his love or lust, containing snapshot photographs, names, and details of women he has ruined. During the evening operation Sherlock Holmes takes the incriminating book from Gruner's rooms. Sir James then carries it away to expose Gruner's moral character and break off his intended marriage to Violet de Merville.

l: evidence against Adelbert Gruner, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: includes Kitty Winter [as a firsthand witness] Evidence against Adelbert Gruner may come from Kitty Winter's firsthand account of how he used and ruined her, her knowledge of his references to other deaths, and his brown leather book documenting ruined women. Holmes considers presenting Kitty personally to Gruner's intended bride.

l: Adelbert Gruner's ruined women, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Adelbert Gruner's ruined women are the subjects of the collection he kept in his brown leather book. The book reportedly contains their photographs, names, and details, and Kitty says Gruner took pride in collecting them.

l: revenge against Adelbert Gruner, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Kitty Winter seeks revenge against Adelbert Gruner by helping Holmes bring him down and see him in the mud. She says that placing him there, with her foot on his face, is all the payment she wants.

l: the interview, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Sherlock Holmes meets Violet de Merville at 104 Berkeley Square, in her father’s yellow-curtained drawing-room, with Miss Winter present. His appeal fails, and the interview ends after Holmes pulls Miss Winter away as she nearly attacks Violet.

l: Violet de Merville's engagement to Baron Gruner, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Violet de Merville’s engagement to Baron Gruner is opposed by her father and Sherlock Holmes because of Gruner’s character, while Violet unwaveringly supports it, dismissing warnings and accusations in belief she can morally improve him.

l: Baron Gruner's mistreatment of women, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: includes tempting and using women [followed by ruining and discarding them] Miss Winter says that Baron Gruner has tempted, used, ruined, and discarded numerous women. She identifies herself as one of his former mistresses and says that Violet may suffer the same fate.

l: Baron Gruner's stormy past, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: includes three entanglements with designing women [as acknowledged by Violet de Merville] Violet acknowledges that Baron Gruner has had a stormy life involving bitter hatred and what she regards as unjust accusations. She says that she knows of three episodes involving women and has been assured that he has sincerely repented.

l: the two attackers, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Two respectably dressed men armed with sticks assault Sherlock Holmes outside the Café Royal, then escape through the Café Royal and Glasshouse Street in an apparently prepared getaway.

l: the attack on Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The attack on Sherlock Holmes occurs outside the Café Royal on Regent Street, where two attackers with sticks inflict scalp wounds and bruises. Holmes exploits the apparent near-fatal injuries, requiring stitches, to make Baron Adelbert Gruner lower his precautions while he prepares a counterplot.

l: the vitriol attack on Baron Gruner, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: uses vitriol [thrown through the window from among the leaves] The vitriol attack on Baron Gruner is carried out by Kitty Winter through an open window. It burns his face, leaves one eye white and glazed and the other red and inflamed, and causes him agonizing pain.

l: Baron Gruner's Chinese collection, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains the Ming saucer [the Baron is considering adding it] Baron Adelbert Gruner's Chinese collection includes Tang, Ming, and other valuable ceramics. He is described as an acknowledged authority on the subject and examines the Ming saucer with intense suspicion and expertise.

l: the Ming saucer, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Ming saucer is a delicate deep-blue piece of genuine egg-shell pottery from the Ming dynasty, one of six corresponding pieces and worth a king's ransom as a complete set. Sherlock Holmes uses it to support Dr. John Watson's false collector identity and entice Baron Adelbert Gruner into receiving him.

l: the newspaper report, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: A newspaper report announces that Sherlock Holmes was murderously assaulted by two men with sticks and is precariously injured; later reports falsely say he is near death with erysipelas, supporting his counterplot.

l: vitriol, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: causes severe facial injuries [to Baron Adelbert Gruner] Vitriol is thrown through Baron Adelbert Gruner's window and eats into his face, ears, and chin. It blinds or severely damages his eyes and leaves his features badly discolored and deformed.

l: Kitty Winter's vitriol-throwing prosecution, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Kitty Winter's vitriol-throwing prosecution begins with a first police-court hearing on a grave charge and ends with the lowest possible sentence after extenuating circumstances emerge at trial.

l: Mr. James M. Dodd, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: James M. Dodd is a big, fresh, sunburned, upstanding Briton, a Throgmorton Street stockbroker and former Imperial Yeoman of the Middlesex Corps during the Boer War. Godfrey Emsworth, his army mate, closest pal, and old comrade, disappears after writing him two letters. Determined to learn his fate, Dodd visits Tuxbury Old Park as a guest, challenges Colonel Emsworth, hears Ralph suggest that Godfrey may be dead or worse, and sees Godfrey pale and altered outside his window. After pursuing him through the garden and investigating a detached lodge, Dodd writes to Sherlock Holmes and becomes his client. He accompanies Holmes to the Hall, insisting on hearing directly that Godfrey is not restrained. The inquiry reveals that Godfrey's seclusion concealed a serious-looking skin condition, not a crime or imprisonment.

l: Godfrey Emsworth, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Godfrey Emsworth, Colonel Emsworth's only son, is a former lance-corporal of B Squadron and a soldier in the Imperial Yeomanry. He served with James M. Dodd in South Africa, where an elephant-gun bullet wounded his shoulder near Diamond Hill outside Pretoria. Afterward he slept in a leper's bed, developed conspicuous white skin patches, and feared leprosy. He stopped writing to Dodd; although the Colonel said he had taken a voyage around the world, he secretly concealed Godfrey in a detached house near the Emsworth home, where Mr. Kent cared for him. Dodd receives letters from Godfrey from Cape Town and Southampton, then sees him furtively near his window and suspects the detached lodge contains him. Godfrey finally appears before Dodd at Tuxbury Old Hall. Sir James Saunders diagnoses non-infective pseudo-leprosy, or ichthyosis, rather than leprosy.

l: Colonel Emsworth, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Colonel Emsworth is a former army officer, Crimean V.C., former martinet, father of his only son Godfrey, and owner of the Emsworth mansion, where he lives with his wife. Strict and intimidating, he conceals Godfrey and the family mystery. He tells James M. Dodd that Godfrey is traveling for his health, refuses details, later confronts a watcher at the detached lodge, and orders Dodd and Holmes away. When Holmes writes “Leprosy,” Emsworth admits the secret and allows them to see Godfrey, explaining that he hid him to prevent compulsory segregation.

l: Ralph, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Ralph is an elderly butler serving at Tuxbury Old Park and the Emsworth mansion. Married and foster-father to Godfrey Emsworth, he remains among the household’s few servants, carrying food to the detached house. His disinfectant-impregnated brown gloves draw Holmes’s attention when Ralph admits Holmes and Dodd.

l: Tuxbury Old Park, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Tuxbury Old Park is the remote Emsworth family property near Bedford, about five miles from the nearest station. Identified in Dodd's letter, it is where Dodd and Holmes investigate Godfrey Emsworth's disappearance and concealment, finding the Emsworth mansion and the detached house where Godfrey lives.

l: Tuxbury Old Hall, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Tuxbury Old Hall is Colonel Emsworth's large, remote country house in Tuxbury Old Park, an old, inaccessible and rambling mansion capable of concealing many people. Its Elizabethan foundations, panelling, tapestry, and old pictures reflect several periods. It contains Emsworth's study and is served by the elderly Ralph and his wife. Dodd stays there with Emsworth and Godfrey's mother; food is carried toward a detached house, and Godfrey finally appears to Dodd there.

l: Godfrey's voyage around the world, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a reported explanation for Godfrey's absence [given by Colonel Emsworth] Godfrey's supposed voyage around the world is the explanation Colonel Emsworth gives for his absence. The Colonel says that Godfrey undertook the voyage because his health was poor after his experiences in Africa, but he refuses to identify the ship, shipping line, or date of departure.

l: the mystery of Godfrey Emsworth's disappearance, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The mystery concerns Godfrey Emsworth's unexplained silence and disappearance from public view after he is wounded in South Africa. His family appears to conceal him: Colonel Emsworth says he is travelling, Ralph wishes him dead, and he is secretly confined in an outhouse or detached house, though he later appears before Dodd. Holmes considers criminal concealment, insanity, and disease, initially infers leprosy, and then obtains a medical review identifying pseudo-leprosy or ichthyosis.

l: Godfrey Emsworth's fate, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_unknown_to James M. Dodd [at the start of the investigation] Godfrey's fate is initially uncertain because his father says he is travelling and Ralph reacts as if his condition is dreadful. Dodd suspects that Godfrey may have been involved in a criminal or disreputable matter, but the unit ends with Godfrey appearing alive before him.

l: the interview between Holmes and James M. Dodd, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: occurs_in January 1903 [at Holmes's rooms] The interview takes place in Holmes's rooms after Dodd urgently seeks his help. Holmes identifies Dodd's background, listens to his account of Godfrey and Tuxbury Old Hall, and learns that Dodd encountered Godfrey immediately after concluding that his friend might be dead or disgraced.

l: the little bearded man, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: A small, brisk, bearded man in a black coat and bowler hat shares a detached lodge with a man identified as Godfrey. He emerges, locks and retains its key, watches the client from the garden, then reads a newspaper and smokes a pipe inside.

l: the garden, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The garden contains several small outhouses and a detached lodge at its far end; the client pursues Godfrey through it, then explores it after hearing a door close.

l: the detached lodge, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The detached lodge is a sizable building at the end of the garden path near the Emsworth mansion, fit for a gardener or gamekeeper. Its shuttered, heavily curtained windows conceal a bright, warm room with a lamp and fire, though a little bearded man and another figure are seen inside. It houses Godfrey Emsworth in seclusion with Mr. Kent; he may leave after dark, and Holmes, Dodd, Colonel Emsworth, and Kent later enter to speak with him.

l: Godfrey's concealment, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a family mystery [involving Godfrey's being hidden from the world] Godfrey appears to be hidden somewhere near the Emsworth house, possibly in the detached lodge. The client believes Colonel Emsworth is concealing him and insists that Godfrey may no longer be a free agent.

l: the client’s intrusion, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a intrusion into family privacy [condemned by Colonel Emsworth] The client follows Godfrey, searches the garden, and spies through the shutter of the detached lodge. Colonel Emsworth calls this conduct a damnable intrusion into the family's privacy and says the client has become a spy rather than remaining a guest.

l: Mr. Kent, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Mr. Kent is a small bearded surgeon and attendant staying with Godfrey Emsworth in a detached house. Bound to secrecy, he helps discuss Godfrey's condition and remains with Godfrey's mother after she faints upon hearing favorable diagnostic news.

l: Sir James Saunders, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Sir James Saunders, a great dermatologist, provides a second medical opinion on Godfrey at Tuxbury Old Park, diagnosing non-infectious pseudo-leprosy or ichthyosis rather than leprosy, an unsightly but possibly curable condition.

l: Godfrey Emsworth's wounding, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: occurs_at the Buffelsspruit morning fight [during the fight outside Pretoria] Godfrey Emsworth was hit by an elephant bullet through the shoulder during a fight at Buffelsspruit outside Pretoria. He remained on his horse until he fainted and later reached a nearby house, where his wound was still bleeding when he awoke.

l: Godfrey Emsworth's exposure to leprosy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: occurs_at the leper hospital [through sleeping in a leper's bed] After being wounded in South Africa, Godfrey reached what he believed was an ordinary house and slept in an unmade bed. He later learned that it was a leper hospital and that he had slept in a leper's bed, leading him to fear that he had contracted leprosy.

l: leprosy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Leprosy is a feared disease initially used to explain Godfrey Emsworth's secrecy, altered appearance, and isolation after he slept in a leper's bed; it can cause lifelong segregation, but Sir James Saunders rules it out.

l: pseudo-leprosy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a skin affection [scale-like, unsightly, and obstinate] Pseudo-leprosy is the diagnosis Sir James Saunders gives for Godfrey's condition. He describes it as a scale-like, unsightly, obstinate, possibly curable, and certainly non-infective affection of the skin.

l: ichthyosis, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a skin affection [scale-like, unsightly, and obstinate] Ichthyosis is identified by Sir James Saunders as another name for Godfrey's condition, described as a scale-like skin affection that resembles leprosy. It is non-infective and may be curable.

l: insanity, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Insanity is one of the three explanations Holmes considers for Godfrey's confinement. Holmes finds it plausible because Mr. Kent appears to act as a keeper and the door is locked, but rejects it because the secrecy and other facts do not fit adequately.

l: segregation of leprosy patients, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Segregation for life among strangers is described as the feared consequence if Godfrey were recognized as having leprosy. Colonel Emsworth and Mr. Kent maintain secrecy to prevent authorities from taking Godfrey away, though the final diagnosis shows that such segregation is unnecessary.

l: the gloves, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: contain the disinfectant [impregnated with it] Ralph's brown leather gloves smell strongly of a tarry disinfectant. Holmes notices the odour when Ralph removes the gloves and concludes that they have been impregnated with disinfectants, supporting his theory that the household is handling a contagious disease.

l: the scrap of paper, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Holmes writes the single word "Leprosy" on a loose sheet and hands it to Colonel Emsworth. The word convinces Colonel Emsworth that Holmes has discovered the family's secret and leads him to permit the party to see Godfrey.

l: the leper hospital, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The leper hospital is a South African institution housing leprosy patients. Godfrey unknowingly enters it wounded, sleeps there, then learns from its medical superintendent that he has been exposed to the disease.

l: the medical diagnosis, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The medical diagnosis is supplied by Sir James Saunders after Holmes brings him to examine Godfrey. It rules out leprosy and identifies pseudo-leprosy, or ichthyosis, a non-infective skin condition that is possibly curable.

l: Billy, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Billy, a young, wise, tactful page, serves and assists Sherlock Holmes at Baker Street, explains the investigation to Dr. John Watson, protects a wax dummy, admits visitors, and brings Sam Merton upstairs amid danger.

l: Lord Cantlemere, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Lord Cantlemere, an old courtier and peer with fifty years of official experience, visits Holmes while doubting and opposing him. Holmes's Mazarin-stone trick briefly leaves Cantlemere in possession of it, showing how he could be arrested; bewildered, Cantlemere withdraws his criticism of Holmes's abilities.

l: Count Negretto Sylvius, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Count Negretto Sylvius is a famous sportsman and game-shot, but chiefly a master criminal and jewel thief. With his accomplice Sam Merton, he is wanted for the Crown diamond burglary and possesses the missing diamond. He later hides the Mazarin stone, plans to send it to Holland for cutting, and tries to deceive Holmes with a false Liverpool location. Visiting Baker Street intending to attack Holmes, he is confronted, exposed, tricked into revealing the stone, and left for police arrest.

l: Sam Merton, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Sam Merton is a professional boxer and criminal accomplice of Count Negretto Sylvius in the Crown diamond burglary. Described as a great, silly, bull-headed gudgeon, he waits outside Baker Street, fears Holmes may be listening, and joins Sylvius's attempt to deceive him. Merton suggests killing Holmes, but after Holmes reveals himself, takes the stone, and arrests them, Merton accepts it as a fair cop.

l: the Crown diamond, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Crown diamond, also called the Mazarin stone, is a great missing yellow jewel valued at one hundred thousand pounds. Count Negretto Sylvius keeps it in a secret pocket, plans to send it out of England and cut it into four pieces in Amsterdam. Holmes links Sylvius and Sam Merton to its theft, takes the diamond, and shows it to Lord Cantlemere.

l: the Mazarin Stone, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_also_known_as the Crown diamond [the great yellow stone] The Mazarin Stone is the great yellow Crown diamond that Sherlock Holmes is trying to recover. Holmes believes Count Negretto Sylvius knows its location and offers to overlook the criminals if they hand it over.

l: the burglary of the Crown diamond, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The hundred-thousand-pound burglary of the Crown diamond brings the Prime Minister and Home Secretary to Baker Street. Committed by Count Negretto Sylvius with Sam Merton, it is investigated by Sherlock Holmes, who identifies witnesses and evidence to recover the stone.

l: the attempted murder of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_attempted_by Count Negretto Sylvius [using a loaded cane and intending to assault Holmes] The attempted murder of Sherlock Holmes is anticipated when Count Negretto Sylvius comes to Baker Street with a loaded cane and a revolver. Holmes avoids the attack with the wax dummy and confronts Sylvius while keeping a weapon ready.

l: the investigation into the Crown diamond, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_conducted_by Sherlock Holmes [for the Crown authorities] The investigation into the Crown diamond leads Sherlock Holmes to follow Count Negretto Sylvius in disguises, observe his connection to the air-gun, and gather evidence against him and Sam Merton. The investigation has trapped both men, but the diamond's location remains unknown.

l: the air-gun, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_made_by Straubenzee [for Count Sylvius] The air-gun was made by Straubenzee and is associated with Count Negretto Sylvius's plan against Sherlock Holmes. Holmes says he believes the weapon is in the opposite window and contrasts it with the noisy revolver.

l: the wax dummy of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The wax dummy of Sherlock Holmes is a lifelike effigy made by the French modeller Tavernier, dressed like Holmes and seated by the Baker Street window. Used by Holmes as a decoy behind a curtain, it convinces watchers and Sam Merton that Holmes is present. Count Negretto Sylvius approaches to strike it, whereupon the real Holmes reveals himself, springs from the chair, and seizes the stone.

l: arrest of the thieves, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The arrest of the thieves follows Holmes capturing the Mazarin stone and summoning police; Count Sylvius and Sam Merton are handcuffed and taken away in a waiting cab.

l: The Adventure of the Three Gables, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a adventure This adventure concerns Sherlock Holmes's investigation of suspicious attempts to acquire The Three Gables and everything inside it. The case begins with intimidation by Steve Dixie and develops into a search for a hidden object connected with Douglas Maberley.

l: Steve Dixie, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Steve Dixie is a bruiser belonging to the Spencer John gang and allegedly involved in killing young Perkins. Ordered by Barney Stockdale, he enters Holmes's rooms to warn him off the Harrow Weald case, but Holmes intimidates him and extends protection to Mrs. Maberley and her house.

l: Barney Stockdale, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Barney Stockdale is the astute leader of a gang, and Steve Dixie’s immediate superior. Hired by Isadora Klein to recover Douglas Maberley’s manuscript, he carries information about Mrs. Maberley’s letter; he, Susan, and his associates are pursued by police after the burglary.

l: Mrs. Maberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Mrs. Maberley is an elderly, refined woman living at and owning The Three Gables, where she employs Susan and keeps the unpacked luggage of her dead son, Douglas. Planning long-dreamed-of travel, possibly to Madeira or around the world, she asks Sherlock Holmes to investigate strange events tied to a proposed sale of her house and contents. After ignoring Holmes's protection advice, she is chloroformed and injured in a burglary, but Holmes obtains £5,000 from Isadora Klein for her travels.

l: Douglas Maberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Douglas Maberley, Mrs. Maberley’s son, was a former attaché at Rome and a novelist whom Holmes remembered as energetic and impressive. He loved Isadora Klein and wished to marry her, but her rejection and violence against him left him cynical, morose, and heartbroken. He wrote a manuscript recounting their relationship under other names as a threat to her reputation, then died suddenly of pneumonia in Rome.

l: Susan Stockdale, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Susan Stockdale, Mrs. Maberley’s servant and Barney Stockdale’s wife, infiltrates The Three Gables. After posting Mrs. Maberley’s letter to Holmes and speaking with Barney over the hedge, she passes him information. Holmes exposes her role; she angrily leaves, refusing to name the person behind Barney, while Mrs. Maberley suspects she enabled the burglars’ entry.

l: The Three Gables house, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Three Gables is Mrs. Maberley’s poorly situated but well-furnished brick-and-timber villa in Harrow Weald, standing on its own acre near Weald Station. A suspicious buyer seeks the house, its furniture, and everything inside, prompting Holmes’s protection. During the night it is burgled by men searching Douglas Maberley’s belongings; police examine it and find a crumpled manuscript fragment.

l: Harrow Weald, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains The Three Gables house Harrow Weald is the location of The Three Gables and the case that prompts threats against Holmes. Holmes travels there with Watson and investigates the people attempting to obtain the house.

l: the Harrow Weald case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: concerns The Three Gables house The Harrow Weald case concerns the unexplained effort to obtain The Three Gables and its contents. The effort is serious enough to involve intimidation, surveillance, Susan's betrayal, and the gang associated with Steve Dixie and Barney Stockdale.

l: the proposed sale of The Three Gables, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: A supposed house agent offers Mrs. Maberley more than she paid for The Three Gables and a large sum for its furniture, insisting on everything and inspecting removals. Because the agreement restricts removing possessions, Mrs. Maberley rejects it.

l: the intimidation of Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Steve Dixie, acting on Barney Stockdale’s orders, warns Holmes that his life is unsafe if he goes to Harrow or interferes in the Harrow Weald case.

l: Douglas Maberley's death, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Douglas Maberley dies in Rome of pneumonia, following a period made moody, morose, and cynical by a love affair. Afterward, Isadora Klein fears a manuscript about their relationship will become public through his effects and orders a burglary.

l: the house-agent scheme, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_conducted_by Haines-Johnson [using the role of auctioneer and valuer] A man calling himself Haines-Johnson, Auctioneer and Valuer, presents Mrs. Maberley with an agreement to sell The Three Gables and all its contents to a client. Holmes doubts that the man is a legitimate house agent and concludes that the scheme is designed to obtain something Mrs. Maberley does not know she possesses.

l: Douglas Maberley's luggage, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Douglas Maberley’s trunks and cases, labeled Milano and Lucerne, arrive from Italy at The Three Gables, remain unpacked, and become central to Holmes’s explanation for sudden interest in the house.

l: Mrs. Maberley's letter to Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Mrs. Maberley’s letter to Sherlock Holmes requests advice about strange incidents at The Three Gables; though postmarked 10 p.m., Susan’s rapid disclosure apparently leads to threats by morning.

l: the house's hidden valuable, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_sought_by the proposed buyer of The Three Gables [the owner does not know she has it] Holmes initially considers whether something valuable may have been buried or hidden in the house, but he rejects that explanation as insufficient because the conspirators also want the furniture. He later suspects that an unknown object, probably newly brought into the house, is valuable to someone but unknown to Mrs. Maberley.

l: Isadora Klein, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Isadora Klein is a celebrated Spanish beauty, widow of the German sugar king Klein, planning to marry the Duke of Lomond despite their age difference. Formerly Douglas Maberley’s lover, she hires Barney Stockdale’s gang to seize his manuscript, is exposed as their employer, burns her copy when challenged, and pays £5,000 for Mrs. Maberley’s travels.

l: Barney Stockdale's gang, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Barney Stockdale's gang is hired by Isadora Klein to recover Douglas Maberley’s manuscript, burglarizes The Three Gables, chloroforms Mrs. Maberley, searches unsuccessfully, then flees when she and the maid raise the alarm and police pursue.

l: the telegram, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: reports the burglary at The Three Gables [in a message from Sutro] The telegram from Sutro tells Sherlock Holmes to come out at once because his client's house has been burgled and the police are in possession. It brings Holmes and Dr. Watson back to The Three Gables.

l: Douglas Maberley's manuscript, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Douglas Maberley’s manuscript recounts his relationship with Isadora Klein under different names, portraying her conduct. Two copies exist; fearing it threatens her future marriage, Klein hires burglars to locate and destroy the remaining copy.

l: the recovered manuscript fragment, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: A sheet in Douglas Maberley’s handwriting, numbered 245 and found after the burglary, recounts a man’s humiliation, his love’s death, and his desire for revenge, before Isadora Klein burns it.

l: the burglary at The Three Gables, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: targeted Douglas Maberley's manuscript [the burglars searched his baggage for it] The burglary at The Three Gables is carried out to locate Douglas Maberley's manuscript. Mrs. Maberley is chloroformed and injured, the burglars search her son's baggage, and they escape with an unknown bundle while leaving behind the recovered manuscript fragment.

l: Douglas Maberley's beating, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Douglas Maberley was beaten and driven away by Barney Stockdale's gang after Isadora Klein rejected his marriage demands; Klein admits ordering the attack, which Stockdale's men carried out roughly.

l: Robert Ferguson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Robert Ferguson is a former Richmond rugby player and tea broker with Ferguson and Muirhead, living at Cheeseman's in Lamberley. Married with a baby and a son, Jacky, he loves his wife deeply and seeks Holmes's help when he believes she has harmed the baby. Holmes discovers she was protecting the child from poison and that jealous Jacky attacked the baby, devastating Ferguson.

l: the unnamed husband, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: A husband with a fifteen-year-old son by his first wife and a baby by his Peruvian wife marries her quickly, then, seeing blood on the baby and her lips, confronts and confines her, seeking Ferguson's help in distress.

l: the Peruvian wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: A beautiful Peruvian merchant’s daughter, loving and apparently devoted as a wife, has a fiercely jealous nature and curious traits. After twice assaulting Jack and being seen apparently biting her baby, she refuses to explain or speak to her husband. Confined to her room, she is cared for by her longtime maid and friend, Dolores.

l: Jacky Ferguson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Jacky Ferguson is the unnamed husband's fifteen-year-old son by his first wife, a pale, fair-haired, affectionate boy devoted to his father and his mother's memory. A childhood fall left him with a twisted, weak spine and shambling gait. Though the Peruvian wife repeatedly assaults him and says she hates him, his defining conflict is intense jealousy of Ferguson's baby. Holmes concludes that Jacky's cruel, possessive hatred led him to attempt to poison the child, and prescribes a year at sea.

l: Ferguson's baby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Ferguson's baby is a dear, beautiful child under one year old, the child of Robert Ferguson and Ferguson's wife. In a foggy November evening, Ferguson fondles the dark-eyed, golden-haired baby protectively. The child is targeted in an attempted poisoning and suffers a small puncture on the throat from a poisoned arrow, but survives after the poison is sucked out. Mrs. Mason guards the baby day and night.

l: Dolores, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Dolores is a tall, slim, brown-faced South American maid and servant in the Ferguson household, a longtime friend of Ferguson's Peruvian wife. On a foggy November evening, she cares for the ill wife, fears being alone without a doctor, brings Dr. Watson to her, admits Holmes and Ferguson, and hears Holmes explain the case.

l: Mrs. Mason, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Mrs. Mason is Ferguson's baby's devoted nurse. She knows of the attempted poisoning, claims to have seen the Peruvian wife apparently bite the child, tells Ferguson, and refuses to leave the baby night or day. During the child's separation from Ferguson's wife, she continues caring for and protecting it after being told to watch it.

l: Lamberley, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_in Sussex [south of Horsham] Lamberley is identified as being in Sussex, south of Horsham. Holmes and Watson plan to travel there to investigate the case.

l: Cheeseman's, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_in Lamberley Cheeseman's is the address in Lamberley from which Robert Ferguson writes and where the family lives. Holmes expects to learn more about the house and its occupants through a personal investigation.

l: Sussex, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains old houses [including houses named after their builders] Sussex is the county where Lamberley and Cheeseman's are located. The alleged vampiric events occur in this English setting rather than in the foreign places associated with traditional vampire stories.

l: the Adventure of the Sussex Vampire, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a case [concerning an alleged vampire in Sussex] The adventure concerns Holmes and Watson's investigation of alleged vampirism, the Peruvian wife's attacks on the baby, and her assaults on Jack at the family house in Sussex.

l: vampirism, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Vampirism is the suspected explanation in the Ferguson matter: traditional vampires are discussed as grave-bound walking corpses or living blood-drinkers. Holmes rejects the supernatural account, investigates after Ferguson sees his wife with blood on her lips, and finds she was sucking poison from the baby's wound.

l: the alleged vampiric attack on the baby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_alleged_to_involve the Peruvian wife [biting the baby's neck and drinking blood] The alleged attack occurs when the Peruvian wife is reportedly seen leaning over the baby and apparently biting its neck, leaving a small wound and blood on the child, sheet, and her lips. The husband and Mrs. Mason treat the incident as evidence of vampirism, while Holmes considers the matter unresolved.

l: the assaults on Jack, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The assaults on Jack are two apparently unprovoked attacks by the Peruvian wife: she strikes him with a stick and beats him with her hands, says she hates him, and leaves no clear explanation.

l: the family house at Cheeseman's, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Cheeseman's family house contains an unnamed husband, his wife, Jack, the baby, Dolores, Mrs. Mason, and recently hired servants; the wife is confined while the baby is guarded.

l: Ferguson's wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Ferguson's wife, a Peruvian lady and mother of Ferguson's baby, is found feverish, distressed, and avoiding her husband after his suspicions. She had secretly sucked poison from the baby's wound to save the child, fearing the effect on Ferguson. Holmes's explanation clears her, affirming her love and self-sacrificing protection.

l: Carlo, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Carlo, Ferguson's spaniel, develops sudden hind-leg paralysis and is examined by a veterinarian. Holmes treats the illness as evidence that poison was tested on Carlo before use against the baby; Carlo is expected to recover.

l: Ferguson farmhouse, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: An isolated, ancient farmhouse in Sussex, Ferguson farmhouse has a large central room with old furnishings and Ferguson's South American weapons collection. On a foggy November evening, Holmes finds an empty quiver beside a bird-bow, supporting his poisoned-arrow theory.

l: the Ferguson household, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains Ferguson's South American weapons collection The Ferguson household is divided by suspicion after Ferguson believes his wife harmed the baby, while she refuses to see him and asks only for her child. Holmes's explanation reveals that the danger came from Jacky's attempted poisoning and leaves Ferguson and his wife to settle the matter.

l: the poisoned arrow, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains curare [as a possible venom] The poisoned arrow is inferred to have been fired from the small bird-bow kept among the South American weapons in the farmhouse. It pricked the baby's neck, and Holmes believes Jacky used it in an attempt to kill the child.

l: curare, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a poison Curare is mentioned by Holmes as one possible poison with which the arrow may have been dipped. He explains that such venom could have caused the baby's death if Ferguson's wife had not sucked it from the wound.

l: the child's wound, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: A poisoned arrow leaves a small, puckered mark on a baby's neck; Ferguson's wife sucks out the venom, preventing attempted poisoning from killing the baby.

l: the letter to Sherlock Holmes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_dated November 19 The letter to Sherlock Holmes, dated November 19, concerns Robert Ferguson's inquiry about the apparent vampire-related danger. Holmes's November 21 reply states that he investigated the matter and brought it to a satisfactory conclusion.

l: the Ferguson case, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: concerns the attempted poisoning of Ferguson's baby The Ferguson case concerns the apparent vampirism, the baby's wound, Ferguson's suspicion of his wife, and the danger within the household. Holmes resolves it by identifying the poison attack and Jacky's motive.

l: the attempted poisoning of Ferguson's baby, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: uses the poisoned arrow [against Ferguson's baby] The attempted poisoning of Ferguson's baby was carried out with a poisoned arrow that pricked the child's neck. Ferguson's wife discovered the attack and removed the poison by sucking it from the wound, while Holmes attributes the attack to Jacky Ferguson.

l: poisoning, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_the_cause_of the child's wound [suspected by Sherlock Holmes] Poisoning is the actual danger behind the apparent vampire attack. Holmes infers that the poison came from an arrow, may have been curare or a similar drug, and had previously been tested on Carlo.

l: John Garrideb, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: John Garrideb presents himself to Holmes as an American counsellor at law from Moorville, Kansas, organizing a search for two other adult Garridebs so they can claim Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's inheritance. He advertises for Howard Garrideb and persuades Nathan Garrideb to go to Birmingham. Holmes notes his English clothing, London accent, and false details, concludes that he is an American criminal using a fraudulent identity, and identifies him as Killer Evans. The inheritance scheme is revealed as a device to remove Nathan from his apartment; John’s ultimate purpose is investigated.

l: Nathan Garrideb, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Nathan Garrideb is a reclusive collector living at 136 Little Ryder Street, where he keeps a museum-like collection of geological, anatomical, historical, archaeological, and other curious specimens. Rarely leaving except for Sotheby's or Christie's, he seeks the Garrideb fortune to finance further additions. As a required adult Garrideb, he joins the inheritance search, confirms John's story, and agrees to go to Birmingham for proof of Howard Garrideb. Deceived by the three Garridebs scheme, he permits Sherlock Holmes to inspect and enter his apartment. The collapse of the inheritance hope leaves him unrecovered; he is last heard of in a Brixton nursing-home.

l: Howard Garrideb, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Howard Garrideb, a Birmingham agricultural-machinery constructor at Grosvenor Buildings, Aston, is identified by an advertisement as a possible third Garrideb; John claims he completes an inheritance requirement, prompting Nathan to meet him.

l: the Garrideb inheritance search, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a search for three adult men named Garrideb [required by Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's will] The search concerns finding three adult men named Garrideb who can satisfy the conditions of Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's will. John says he has searched throughout the United States and then looked in England, while Holmes questions whether the search is genuine.

l: Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's will, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Alexander Hamilton Garrideb's will divides the Garrideb fortune into three parts, requiring three adult Garrideb men to stand together before inheritance is claimed; John Garrideb's share depends on finding two others.

l: the Garrideb fortune, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Garrideb fortune is an approximately five-million-dollar-per-share inheritance controlled by Alexander Hamilton Garrideb’s will. It can be claimed only after the required Garridebs are found, prompting Nathan’s plans to expand his collection.

l: the Adventure of the Three Garridebs, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: In June 1902, Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson investigate an unusual inheritance search involving John, Nathan, and proposed Howard Garrideb; Holmes suspects deception as Nathan agrees to visit Birmingham.

l: the Howard Garrideb advertisement, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: A local-paper advertisement identifies Howard Garrideb as an Aston agricultural-machinery constructor offering artesian-well estimates; John presents it as proof the third Garrideb has been found.

l: James Winter, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: James Winter, also known as Morecroft and Killer Evans, is a forty-four-year-old Chicago native listed by Scotland Yard after shooting three men in the United States and coming to London.

l: Killer Evans, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Killer Evans, a forty-four-year-old Chicago native and dangerous armed criminal, shot three men, including Rodger Prescott over cards. Under police supervision since 1901, he posed as John Garrideb to reach Prescott's hidden counterfeiting operation, fired at Watson, and was subdued by Holmes and handed to authorities.

l: Rodger Prescott, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Rodger Prescott was a Chicago criminal, forger, and coiner who lived in Nathan Garrideb's apartment as Waldron, leaving a hidden printing operation and counterfeit banknotes beneath it until discovery.

l: Nathan Garrideb's apartment, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Nathan Garrideb's apartment in London, once occupied by Rodger Prescott, hides a secret cellar beneath the floor; Killer Evans uses the three Garridebs deception to search it for counterfeiting equipment.

l: the Garrideb invention, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_devised_by Killer Evans [to remove Nathan Garrideb from his room] The Garrideb invention was a scheme devised by Killer Evans to send Nathan Garrideb away from his apartment. Evans exploited the unusual name and arranged an apparent search for three men named Garrideb, including an advertisement designed to draw Nathan to Birmingham.

l: the secret cellar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains Prescott's counterfeiting outfit The secret cellar was hidden beneath a trapdoor under the central table in Nathan Garrideb's apartment. It contained rusted machinery, rolls of paper, bottles, and bundles of counterfeit banknotes.

l: Prescott's counterfeiting outfit, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Prescott's counterfeiting outfit, a printing press and materials used by Rodger Prescott, was hidden beneath Nathan Garrideb's apartment and discovered after Prescott's death, pleasing police who had failed to locate it.

l: Prescott's counterfeit banknotes, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: number two thousand [worth one hundred each and fit to pass anywhere] Prescott's counterfeit banknotes were arranged in bundles on a table in the secret cellar. Killer Evans said there were two thousand notes worth one hundred each and claimed they were good enough to pass anywhere.

l: the shooting of Rodger Prescott, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: In January 1895, Killer Evans shot Rodger Prescott in a Waterloo Road nightclub; Prescott died, while Evans claimed self-defense and said Prescott planned to flood London with counterfeit banknotes.

l: Watson's wounding, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_caused_by Killer Evans [a gunshot wound to the thigh] Watson's wounding occurred when Killer Evans fired two shots after emerging from the secret cellar. A bullet caused a superficial injury to Watson's thigh, and Holmes found that it was only a scratch.

l: Killer Evans's attempted murder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_committed_by Killer Evans [against Dr. John Watson and Sherlock Holmes] Killer Evans's attempted murder consisted of firing two shots at Dr. John Watson after Holmes and Watson confronted him. Holmes said that, so far as he could see, the charge was attempted murder, and Evans was left for the authorities to deal with.

l: counterfeiting, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Counterfeiting is the criminal activity associated with Rodger Prescott's hidden machinery and banknotes. The recovered operation was regarded by the Yard as a major public danger because the notes were difficult to distinguish from genuine Bank of England notes.

l: the three Garridebs deception, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_an_invention_of Killer Evans [used to get Nathan Garrideb out of his room] The three Garridebs deception was Killer Evans's plan for removing Nathan Garrideb from his apartment without immediately harming him. It used the supposed inheritance connected with several men named Garrideb and sent Nathan on a false journey to Birmingham.

l: Neil Gibson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Neil Gibson is an American senator and the world's greatest gold-mining magnate, a masterful, formidable millionaire whose business power can make or break communities, cities, and nations, usually breaking them. He owns Thor Place in Hampshire, employs Marlow Bates as estate manager, has enemies, is violent, and keeps a loaded revolver beside his bed amid a large firearms collection. He married Maria Pinto after meeting her in Brazil, but his love faded; he became harsh toward her, with Bates and others calling his treatment brutal. Grace Dunbar then entered his life. Gibson passionately desired her, told her he wanted her love and possession, and, though unable to marry her, offered money to secure her comfort. Grace nevertheless influenced him powerfully for good, and Gibson later says he is thankful his plans failed and promises she will never again be molested. When Mrs. Gibson dies near the bridge at Thor Place, Gibson returns, calls for a doctor and police, and is said to have been in his library rather than outside after returning from town. A missing matching pistol and his alleged offences toward Grace raise suspicion, but he comes to Sherlock Holmes seeking evidence to prove Grace innocent. He initially denies a personal connection to her, then admits his feelings, accepts Holmes's reproach calmly, and expects Holmes to establish her innocence.

l: Miss Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Miss Grace Dunbar is a young, beautiful governess employed under the millionaire's roof to educate his two children. Described as a tall brunette with a strong, sensitive face and innate nobility, she has a powerful beneficial influence over the Gold King and opposes wealth built on the ruin of thousands. Her position collapses into a murder accusation when Mrs. Gibson is shot. A note signed by Miss Dunbar arranged a meeting at Thor Bridge, she was seen near the bridge and admits writing the note and being there, and a revolver matching the fatal bullet is found in her wardrobe. She initially reserves her defence on her lawyer's advice. She later tells Holmes that Mrs. Gibson hated her, secretly summoned her to Thor Bridge, and angrily confronted her there. Miss Dunbar denies knowing of the pistol, while the millionaire insists she is innocent and Holmes suspects it was planted to incriminate her. Holmes works to vindicate her from the charge.

l: Maria Pinto, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Maria Pinto, a Brazilian and daughter of a Manaos government official, was Neil Gibson's devoted wife. Once exceptionally beautiful and passionate, she was found dead near Thor Bridge in her dinner dress, fatally shot through the brain.

l: Marlow Bates, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Marlow Bates, Neil Gibson’s neurotic estate manager and employee, warns Holmes that Gibson brutally treated his wife; after giving notice, he plans to leave within weeks and says he does not know how she died.

l: Thor Bridge, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Thor Bridge is a broad, balustraded stone bridge carrying the drive across the narrowest part of Thor Mere, a long reedy pool in the grounds of Thor Place. It matters as the site where Mrs. Gibson meets Miss Dunbar, where Mrs. Gibson's body is found at the bridge's mouth, and where Miss Dunbar is seen near the time of the shooting. A fresh, forceful chip in its parapet leads Holmes to demonstrate a string-dragged, stone-weighted pistol striking the bridge and falling into the water.

l: Thor Mere, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a sheet of water [long, deep, and reed-girt] Thor Mere is a long, deep, reed-girt sheet of water crossed by Thor Bridge. The tragedy occurred at the bridge over this mere.

l: Winchester, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: contains Miss Dunbar's trial and charge [formal proceedings] Sherlock Holmes, Dr. John Watson, and Mr. Joyce Cummings spend the night at Winchester because the formalities have not been completed. Holmes interviews Miss Dunbar in her cell there and develops the clue that leads to the solution.

l: Mrs. Gibson's killing, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Mrs. Gibson's killing is a tragedy at Thor Bridge involving the death of Neil Gibson's wife, Maria Pinto. Found late at night in dinner dress and a shawl, she had been shot behind the right temple at close range; no weapon or signs of struggle were present. Although staged as a murder to implicate Miss Dunbar, the death is determined to have been a carefully planned suicide: after confronting Miss Dunbar, Mrs. Gibson fatally shot herself and disposed of the pistol in the water beside the bridge.

l: the murder, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The murder was committed with a revolver, though no weapon was found near the body. Authorities attribute it to Miss Dunbar based on evidence, while Holmes suspects concealed facts.

l: the alleged attack on Miss Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The alleged attack on Miss Dunbar is the case leading to her murder charge and referral to the Assizes at Winchester. Coroner's-jury and police-court proceedings found the evidence persuasive, including a revolver hidden in her wardrobe and a note left at the scene. Miss Dunbar reserves her defence and is represented by Joyce Cummings. Neil Gibson hires Holmes, whose reconstruction suggests the Gold King's wife threatened Miss Dunbar, a scuffle followed, and the shooting was accidental.

l: the problem of Thor Bridge, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The Problem of Thor Bridge concerns Sherlock Holmes’s investigation of Mrs. Gibson’s apparent murder. Suspicion falls on Neil Gibson and Miss Dunbar, while the missing weapon, Dunbar’s connection to the scene, and concealed relationships complicate the case. Holmes finds inconsistencies suggesting planted evidence, uses a chip in the bridge’s fresh stonework to trace disposal of the weapon, identifies Mrs. Gibson’s motive, and resolves the attempt to make Miss Dunbar appear guilty.

l: the letter from Neil Gibson, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Neil Gibson writes Sherlock Holmes desperately seeking help to prevent Miss Dunbar’s execution, declaring her certainly innocent and offering all his resources to save her.

l: the revolver, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: A revolver with one discharged chamber was found on the floor of Miss Dunbar's wardrobe, a circumstance said to incriminate her. Its calibre matched the bullet that killed Neil Gibson's wife. The Gold King proposes that his wife carried it to frighten Miss Dunbar, that it discharged in a scuffle, and that she later hid or discarded it among her clothes. Neil Gibson also keeps numerous firearms and sleeps beside a loaded revolver.

l: the bullet, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: matched the revolver [in calibre] The bullet passed through the brain of Neil Gibson's wife. Its calibre matched that of the revolver found in Miss Dunbar's wardrobe.

l: Miss Dunbar's note, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Miss Dunbar's note, addressed to Mrs. Gibson, arranges a nine o'clock appointment at Thor Bridge and is signed “G. Dunbar.” Mrs. Gibson is found clutching it in her left hand at death. The note becomes direct evidence against the governess, though the clutching suggests it was not planted after death.

l: the murder investigation, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: concerns the fatal shooting of Maria Pinto The murder investigation established that the victim was found near Thor Bridge late at night and that no weapon was beside her. It also gathered the revolver, the note, Miss Dunbar's presence near the bridge, and the possible motive involving Neil Gibson.

l: the fatal shooting of Maria Pinto, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The fatal shooting of Maria Pinto is identified with the death of Neil Gibson's wife, who was found with a revolver bullet through her brain. The text does not establish who fired the shot, although Miss Dunbar has been accused.

l: the love affair between Neil Gibson and Miss Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: The alleged love affair between Neil Gibson and Miss Dunbar is presented as a possible motive because Gibson was said to have shown the governess pressing attentions and she might benefit if his wife died. Gibson initially denies any relationship with her, while his emotional letter to Holmes leads Holmes to suspect that she is important to him.

l: Thor Place, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Thor Place is Mr. Neil Gibson’s estate in Hampshire, with a half-timbered house combining Tudor and Georgian features, grounds, pheasant preserves, and Gibson’s firearms. After a delay and a night at Winchester, Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson travel there, inspect the weapons after examining Thor Bridge, and then proceed toward the crime scene.

l: the millionaire's romantic desire for Grace Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: is_a passionate regard The millionaire says he could not live under the same roof as Grace and remain in daily contact with her without feeling passionate regard for her. He told her that he wanted to marry her and that he had never wanted anything more than her love and possession.

l: evidence, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: concerns the millionaire's case The millionaire says he came to Holmes with a question of evidence rather than a question of morals. The unit does not specify what the evidence is.

l: morality, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: Holmes distinguishes the question of morality from the question of evidence and criticizes the millionaire's admitted conduct. The millionaire says he is not pretending to be better than he is and objects to Holmes's moral criticism.

l: the millionaire's alleged offences against Grace Dunbar, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
s: include trying to ruin Grace Dunbar [while she was under his roof] Holmes says the millionaire has admitted trying to ruin a defenseless girl who was under his roof. Holmes suggests that this conduct may be no better than anything Grace is accused of doing.

l: the Gold King's wife, The Case-Book of Sherlock Holmes
